what: 3.9 Working with plant pedigrees and selfing
title: 1. How to tidy a pedigree
text: plant breeding, many species monoecious — single plant produces male female gametes can serve male (sire) female (dam) parent. Self-fertilization (selfing) common practice crops rice, wheat, soybean, maize. pedigree, selfing appears individual listed Sire Dam one offspring. selfing parameter tidyped() controls pedigrees handled: selfing = FALSE (default): Treats individual appearing Sire Dam sex conflict returns error. mode suitable animal pedigrees bisexuality data error. selfing = TRUE: Allows individual Sire Dam. individuals automatically assigned Sex = "monoecious", pedigree metadata records status. following example demonstrates typical self-pollinating plant breeding scenario: Setting selfing = TRUE resolves issue. monoecious individuals (F1, F2_1) automatically identified, sex assigned accordingly: summary() method reports count monoecious individuals: tidied output: - P1 → male (appears Sire) - P2 → female (appears Dam) - F1 → monoecious (appears Sire Dam F2_1, F2_2) - F2_1 → monoecious (appears Sire Dam F3) Self-fertilization produces inbred offspring: inbreeding coefficient f = 0.5 individuals derived single generation selfing, increases successive selfing generations (f = 0.75 F3). code: library(visPedigree)  # Example 1: Tidy and visualize a small pedigree # Use compact = TRUE to condense eligible full-sib groups into a green-grey # family-summary rectangle labelled FS×N. cands <- c("Y", "Z1", "Z2") small_ped |>   tidyped(cand = cands) |>   visped(compact = TRUE)  # Example 2: Relationship Matrices (v1.0.0+) # Compute the additive relationship matrix (A) using high-performance C++ algorithms. # Use compact = TRUE to accelerate calculation for pedigrees with large full-sib families. mat_a <- simple_ped |> tidyped() |> pedmat(method = "A", compact = TRUE) # Visualize the relationship matrix as a heatmap with histograms vismat(mat_a)  # Apply A to candidate contribution weights without constructing A tp_simple <- tidyped(simple_ped) candidate_weights <- c(J5X804 = 0.5, J3Y620 = 0.5) weighted_relationship <- pedprod(tp_simple, candidate_weights)  # Example 3: Inbreeding & Highlighting # Calculate inbreeding coefficients (f) and display them on the graph (e.g., "ID (0.05)"). # Specific individuals can be highlighted to track their inheritance paths. simple_ped |>   tidyped(inbreed = TRUE) |>   visped(highlight = "J5X804", trace = "up", showf = TRUE, compact = TRUE)  # Example 4: Pedigree Analysis (v1.4.0+) # Summarize pedigree structure tp <- tidyped(big_family_size_ped) tp |>   pedstats(timevar="Year")  # Summarize diversity-related indicators ref_ind <- tp[Gen == max(Gen), Ind] tp |>   pediv(reference = ref_ind)  # Example 5: Pedigree Splitting # Automatically split the pedigree into independent sub-populations (connected groups). # Each group is returned as a standalone tidyped object for separate analysis. split_list <- simple_ped |> tidyped() |> splitped() summary(split_list[[1]])

title: Calculate Effective Population Size — pedne
text: effective population size can calculated using one three methods: "coancestry" (Default): Based rate coancestry (\(f_{ij}\))   pairs individuals. context, \(f_{ij}\) probability two alleles   randomly sampled individuals $$ $j$ identical descent, equivalent   half additive genetic relationship (\(f_{ij} = a_{ij} / 2\)).   method generally robust accounts full genetic drift   bottlenecks (Cervantes et al., 2011).   $$\Delta c_{ij} = 1 - (1 - c_{ij})^{1/(\frac{ECG_i + ECG_j}{2})}$$   $$N_e = \frac{1}{2 \overline{\Delta c}}$$   handle large populations, method samples nsamples individuals per cohort   computes mean rate coancestry among . Sampled relationship   coefficients obtained batched matrix-free \(AX\) products,   full additive relationship matrix constructed. "inbreeding": Based individual rate inbreeding ($F_i$) (Gutiérrez et al., 2008, 2009).   $$\Delta F_i = 1 - (1 - F_i)^{1/(ECG_i - 1)}$$   $$N_e = \frac{1}{2 \overline{\Delta F}}$$ "demographic": Based demographic census breeding males females (Wright, 1931).   $$N_e = \frac{4 N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f}$$   \(N_m\) \(N_f\) number unique male female parents contributing cohort.
